summary: Jane Eyre, an orphan, is raised unkindly by her aunt at Gateshead and sent to Lowood, a harsh charity school where she loses her friend Helen Burns. She becomes a governess at Thornfield Hall and falls in love with her moody employer, Edward Rochester. On their wedding day she learns he already has a wife, who is locked in the attic. Jane flees, nearly starves, and is taken in at Moor House by the clergyman St John Rivers and his sisters. When a mysterious call reaches her, she returns to Thornfield and finds Rochester blind and free.
context: Charlotte Bronte published Jane Eyre as 'Currer Bell' through Smith, Elder & Co. of London on 19 October 1847. It was a success at once. Critics noted its first-person voice, which follows Jane's moral and spiritual growth from the inside. Lowood was drawn from the Clergy Daughters' School at Cowan Bridge, where Bronte's two elder sisters fell ill and died. The book touches class, religion, sexuality and the limits placed on women, and the BBC's Big Read poll of 2003 ranked it tenth among Britain's best-loved books.

people.name: Charlotte Bronte
people.note: Born 1816, eldest surviving of the Bronte sisters; she published under the name Currer Bell.

people.name: Jane Eyre
people.note: The orphan narrator, who grows from a mistreated child to an independent woman.

people.name: Edward Rochester
people.note: Master of Thornfield Hall, whose secret marriage nearly ruins Jane's life.

people.name: St John Rivers
people.note: Earnest, cold clergyman and Jane's cousin, who proposes to her.

people.name: Helen Burns
people.note: Jane's friend at Lowood, who bears injustice with patience.

people.name: Mrs Reed
people.note: Jane's aunt, who abuses her at Gateshead Hall.

people.name: Smith, Elder & Co.
people.note: London firm that published the novel in October 1847.

places.name: Cowan Bridge, Lancashire
places.note: Site of the Clergy Daughters' School that Bronte used as the model for Lowood.

places.name: Mirfield (Roe Head)
places.note: Where Bronte attended school in 1831 and taught from 1835.

places.name: Brussels
places.note: Bronte studied and taught at the Heger Pensionnat here from 1842.

places.name: London
places.note: Home of Smith, Elder & Co., first publisher of the book.

ideas.title: Independence and equality
ideas.note: Jane insists on being treated as a free human being, whatever her rank or looks.

ideas.title: Inner life told in first person
ideas.note: The book was among the first to centre on one person's moral and spiritual development.

ideas.title: Duty against passion
ideas.note: Rochester offers love without honesty and St John offers duty without love; Jane refuses both on those terms.

ideas.title: Class and the governess
ideas.note: Jane's position as a poor, educated woman shows how fragile and constrained such lives were.

passages.quote: There was no possibility of taking a walk that day.
passages.why: The plain opening line, setting a restless, confined child.

passages.quote: Do you think, because I am poor, obscure, plain, and little, I am soulless and heartless? You think wrong!⁠—I have as much soul as you⁠—and full as much heart!
passages.why: Jane's outburst against Rochester's assumption that she can be kept or dismissed.

passages.quote: I am no bird; and no net ensnares me; I am a free human being with an independent will, which I now exert to leave you.
passages.why: Her declaration of independence, stated plainly.

passages.quote: I would always rather be happy than dignified
passages.why: Jane chooses warmth over St John's cold propriety.

passages.quote: Reader, I married him. A quiet wedding we had: he and I, the parson and clerk, were alone present.
passages.why: The famous direct address that opens the ending.
